title: Rory and the Sunstone Mirror
markdown:
Rory was a badger cub who knew his tunnels better than his own paws. Anything that made him feel wobbly? Not so much. He lived in the Whispering Woods, and the woods had earned the name. Every leaf rustle, every bird chirp, every soft sigh of breeze sounded like secrets being traded. He loved it. Most of all he loved digging. His paws were tiny efficient shovels. The tunnels were cozy, dark, and blessedly safe—until the sun began its daily descent. As that fiery ball stretched golden arms lower, the shadows stretched too: long, wiggly, spooky things that turned friendly trees into grumpy giants and innocent bushes into lurking monsters. His whiskers twitched with a very particular kind of worry.

His best friend was Kite, a fox cub: whirlwind of bright eyes, perky ears, fur the colour of ripe apricot, a splash of sunshine zipping through the greenery. “Come on, Rory! The Sunken Meadow! Dragonflies with wings like stained glass!”

One dazzling afternoon they played Follow the Beetle near the Standing Stones: ancient grey titans, worn smooth by centuries, humming with a quiet old magic that tickled toes even when you stood still. As the sun slid toward the horizon and painted orange and pink, something extraordinary happened.

WHOOSH.

From the tip-top of the tallest stone a single impossibly bright line of light, like a golden crayon drawn by a giant, shot straight across the field. It pulsed with a warmth that made the air shimmer.

“Crikey!” Kite’s ears shot up. His amber eyes held the beam.

Then, as if someone had flicked a switch, a shadow fell. Not any shadow: a dimming one. Cheerful chirps faltered. The woods’ whispers faded to faint sighs. Professor Hoot, the oldest owl, landed with a gentle thump, wise eyes blinking slowly.

“Oh dear. The Sun King’s gift. A fleeting thing. That light keeps the spirit of our woods alive. Flowers bloom. Streams chuckle. But it will be gone when the sun sets. If it is not kept—the whispers fade to silence. Colours dim. Joy seeps away.”

Rory felt a prickle, sharp and cold. Fading light? Silence? His tummy flip-flopped. The burrow called.

“Why is it like this, Professor?” Kite’s tail drooped.

“A challenge. The Sun King left a riddle. The stones align with the solstice sun, pointing the way. To keep the light’s magic it must be reflected. A special mirror, hidden deep, can catch this beam and send it to a secret hollow. Without it the light is lost, and with it the heart of the woods.”

“A mirror to catch the light! Where?”

Professor Hoot’s golden eyes blinked. “That is the next part of the puzzle. Find it. Be quick. The sun waits for no one.”

Another thump, and he was gone. A race against time, heavy as a damp log.

Kite was already sniffing. “This way! Something old and shiny!” He darted toward a dense tangle of brambles at the roots of an ancient gnarled oak.

Rory followed, paws heavy as if through treacle. Shadows stretched like spooky fingers. He remembered Granny: shadows are just the absence of light; they make trees look like monsters, but they’re only pretend. Pretend or not, his heart performed an extra beat.

Kite’s triumphant yip cut the stillness. “Found it!”

Nestled among mossy roots, half-hidden by fallen leaves: a mirror polished smooth as a river stone, seeming to capture every glimmer of fading sun. The Sunstone Mirror. It hummed faintly with captured glow.

“Brilliant,” Rory breathed, fear forgotten for a flicker.

“Professor said a secret hollow. Every second counts!”

They were off. Kite a blur over roots. Rory’s short badger legs pumping. Under dense clumps the light dimmed further; his heart drummed. The woods grew softer. The whispers became hesitant murmurs.

Kite was fast. Rory was a badger. He knew the ground. He could feel hollows beneath his paws, tell where earth might give way to an underground passage. He understood the earth in a way Kite, sky-and-surface, never could.

They ran and ran, breaths coming in little puffs in the cooling air. The sun was a fiery orange ball sinking lower and lower toward the distant hills. The golden beam from the Standing Stones, though weaker, still cut a determined path across the field. They knew they had to catch it and send it to that special hollow before the last ray of sunshine vanished. A blackbird tried one last song and thought better of it. The brambles caught at Rory’s fur as if the woods themselves wanted one more minute.

“Nearly there!” Kite pointed his nose at a small moss-covered depression near a cluster of bluebells that seemed to be wilting. “Hollow near colourful flowers!”

They tumbled in, paws scrabbling. The beam was thin now, a pale ribbon of fading gold. Rory clutched the mirror, paws trembling. The hollow felt darker, more enclosed, musty, his own thump in his ears. He saw his shaky reflection, eyes wide. A little voice: what if you are too scared to hold it steady?

“Rory?” Kite sat beside him, bright eyes on his face. “You dig the most amazing tunnels. They’re dark, aren’t they? Darker than this, sometimes. But you never get scared when you’re digging.”

Rory looked at Kite, then at the mirror. His tunnels. His dark. His space that he had made. Safe.

He took a deep breath, drawing in the cool earthy scent of the woods. Tightened his grip, paws surprisingly steady. Granny’s pretend shadows. He was a badger. A digger. Brave enough to make his own light, just as he made his own tunnels. The whispers of fear in his head would not be louder than the hopeful hum of the Sunstone Mirror. Kite did not hurry him. The hollow waited, and so did the beam.

He adjusted the mirror, paws firm. The faint beam caught the polish. He angled it toward the hollow’s edge, toward the bluebells, as Professor Hoot had described.

A heart-stopping moment: nothing. The sun dipped. The light flickered. His tummy flipped. He felt Kite’s hopeful gaze.

Then WHOOSH.

The reflected beam shot out, a perfect thin golden arrow, landing in the centre of the bluebell patch. The flowers stood tall, petals shimmering with inner light. The woods’ whispers surged back, stronger, joyful, as if the trees sighed in relief. The air seemed to sing.

The sun dipped below the horizon, a last sliver of warmth, but the light in the Whispering Woods remained, vibrant, alive.

Rory let out a shaky laugh of relief and joy. He had not only held the mirror. He had faced the dimming, the long shadows, the wobbly feelings.

Kite nudged him, tail wagging with all its might. “Told you. Brave enough to dig your way out of any dark corner. Best light-catcher in the whole woods.”

Rory grinned a real confident badger grin. The woods were lively and whispering again. Even explorers who love tunnels sometimes feel a little scared. What you do with the wobble is the rest of the story. He had shone a light, and the shadows—pretend after all—had gone back to being only trees.
